summary: Optimistic Duplicate Address Detection modifies IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and Stateless Address Autoconfiguration. It aims to cut address configuration delays when no conflict exists, limit disruption when one does, and stay interoperable with unmodified hosts and routers. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: When an IPv6 device joins a network, it normally has to wait for a duplicate address check to finish before it may use its new address. This RFC lets it use the address straight away and finish the check in the background, with strict rules that stop it from disturbing another device that already owns the same address.

questions: what is an optimistic address in ipv6
how does ipv6 duplicate address detection work
subtitle: Let a host use its new IPv6 address at once, and check for duplicates afterwards.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 host has to wait for Duplicate Address Detection to finish before it can use a new address, and that wait is long enough to disrupt time-critical services on links where hosts attach and detach often.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an Optimistic address state: the address is usable immediately while the usual Neighbor Solicitation check runs in the background, and the rules that limit disruption to the rightful owner of a duplicated address.
tldr.outcome: Address configuration happens without the RetransTimer delay, and the document shows that the added risk is very small when the address comes from a random or well-distributed identifier.

today: RFC 4429 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 7527, Enhanced Duplicate Address Detection, which builds on the Optimistic address state defined here. The memo does not itself change the security properties of Neighbor Discovery, and Secure Neighbor Discovery remains the mechanism that protects the protocol.

sections.title: The Problem and the Goal
sections.content:
Optimistic Duplicate Address Detection is a modification of the existing IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and Stateless Address Autoconfiguration processes. Its intention is to minimize address configuration delays in the successful case and to reduce disruption as far as possible in the failure case. It is useful because in most cases Duplicate Address Detection is far more likely to succeed than fail, and disruption is minimized by limiting a node's participation in Neighbor Discovery while its addresses are still Optimistic.

The memo is explicit that it does not intend to improve the security, reliability or robustness of Duplicate Address Detection beyond that of existing standards, but merely to make it faster. The existing address configuration mechanisms provide adequate collision detection for the fixed hosts they were designed for, but a growing population of nodes needs continuous network access despite frequently changing their network attachment.

An optimized method needs to provide interoperability with nodes using the current standards, remove the RetransTimer delay during address configuration, ensure that the probability of address collision is not increased, improve the resolution mechanisms for address collisions, and minimize disruption in the case of a collision. Merely reducing RetransTimer is not sufficient, because values of RetransTimer long enough to guarantee detection of a collision are too long to avoid disruption of time-critical services.
sections.plainLanguage: Standard duplicate address checking makes a new device wait before it can talk. That wait protects everyone, but on a busy wireless link it is too slow for services that cannot pause. This RFC keeps the check but removes the wait.

sections.title: The Optimistic Address State
sections.content:
RFC 2462 introduced a tentative address, an address whose uniqueness on a link is being verified before its assignment to an interface. A tentative address is not considered assigned to an interface in the usual sense: an interface discards received packets addressed to it, but accepts Neighbor Discovery packets related to Duplicate Address Detection for it. A preferred address is assigned to an interface whose use by upper-layer protocols is unrestricted. A deprecated address is assigned but its use is discouraged rather than forbidden, and packets sent to or from it are still delivered as expected.

This memo introduces a new address state, Optimistic, that marks an address which is available for use but has not completed Duplicate Address Detection. Unless noted otherwise, components of the IPv6 protocol stack should treat addresses in the Optimistic state equivalently to those in the Deprecated state, indicating that the address is available for use but should not be used if another suitable address is available. Implementations should treat an Optimistic address as if it were Deprecated, and if address states are recorded as individual flags this is easily achieved by also setting Deprecated when Optimistic is set.

The address lifetime rules of RFC 2462 still apply, so an address may be Deprecated as well as Optimistic. When Duplicate Address Detection completes without incident, the address becomes either a Preferred or a Deprecated address, as per RFC 2462.
sections.plainLanguage: The new state, Optimistic, means the address is ready to use but not yet checked. Software that chooses which address to send from should treat it like a deprecated address, so it only uses it when no better one is available.

sections.title: Avoiding Disruption
sections.content:
To avoid interference, an Optimistic Node must not send any messages from an Optimistic address that would override its neighbours' Neighbor Cache entries for the address it is trying to configure, because doing so would disrupt the rightful owner of the address in the case of a collision.

Three rules achieve this. The Override flag is cleared in Neighbor Advertisements sent from Optimistic addresses, which prevents neighbours from overriding their existing Neighbor Cache entries; the Override flag is already defined in RFC 2461 and used for Proxy Neighbor Advertisement. Neighbor Solicitations are never sent from an Optimistic address, because they include a Source Link-Layer Address Option that may cause Neighbor Cache disruption; Neighbor Solicitations sent as part of Duplicate Address Detection are sent from the unspecified address, without such an option. And an Optimistic address is never used as the source address of a Router Solicitation with a Source Link-Layer Address Option; another address, or the unspecified address, may be used, or the solicitation may be sent without the option.

An address collision with a router may cause a neighbouring router's IsRouter flags for that address to be cleared. However, routers do not appear to use the IsRouter flag for anything, and the Neighbor Advertisement sent in response to the collision reasserts the flag.
sections.plainLanguage: While the check is running, the new device must not disturb anyone else. So its neighbour advertisements carry a cleared override flag, it never sends neighbour solicitations from the new address, and it leaves the link-layer address out of its router solicitations.

sections.title: The Rules That Change the Standards
sections.content:
All normative text in the memo is contained in this section. The general rule is that Optimistic Duplicate Address Detection should only be used when the implementation is aware that the address is based on a most likely unique interface identifier, generated randomly, produced by a well-distributed hash function, or assigned by DHCPv6. It should not be used for manually entered addresses.

The changes to RFC 2461, Neighbor Discovery, are these. A node must not send a Router Solicitation with a Source Link-Layer Address Option from an Optimistic address; router solicitations should be sent from a non-Optimistic or the unspecified address, though they may be sent from an Optimistic address as long as the option is not included. A node must not use an Optimistic address as the source address of a Neighbor Solicitation. If the node is not told the router's link-layer address in a Router Advertisement and cannot determine it without breaking these rules, it must leave the address Tentative until Duplicate Address Detection completes, despite being unable to send any packets to the router. And when a node has a unicast packet to send from an Optimistic address to a neighbour whose link-layer address it does not know, it must not perform Address Resolution; it should forward the packet to a default router on the link in the hope that the packet will be redirected, or otherwise buffer it until the check is complete.

The changes to RFC 2462, Stateless Address Autoconfiguration, are these. A host may choose to configure a new address as Optimistic, but a host that does not know the router's link-layer address should not do so, and a router should not configure an Optimistic address. The host must join the all-nodes multicast address and the solicited-node multicast address of the tentative address, and should not delay before sending Neighbor Solicitation messages. The Optimistic address is configured and available for use on the interface immediately and must be flagged Optimistic. When Duplicate Address Detection completes the address is no longer Optimistic and becomes Preferred or Deprecated according to RFC 2462. The node must not reply to a Neighbor Solicitation for an Optimistic address from the unspecified address, because receipt of such a solicitation indicates the address is a duplicate and it must be deconfigured. The node must reply to a Neighbor Solicitation for an Optimistic address from a unicast address, but the reply must have the Override flag cleared.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists the exact changes to the two IPv6 standards it builds on. The big one is that the address may be used the moment it is configured. The rest are limits on what the host may send while the check runs, and on what happens if a duplicate turns up.

sections.title: How It Behaves in Practice
sections.content:
All the cases consider an Optimistic Node receiving a Router Advertisement containing a new prefix and deciding to autoconfigure a new Optimistic address on that prefix. The node immediately sends a Neighbor Solicitation to determine if its new address is already in use.

In the non-collision case, the address being configured is unused and not present in any neighbour's Neighbor Cache. There is no response to the solicitation, which is sent from the unspecified address and does not modify neighbours' caches. The node already has the router's link-layer address from the Router Advertisement, and the router can determine the node's link-layer address through standard Address Resolution. Communications can begin as soon as the two have each other's link-layer addresses. After the appropriate delay has completed, the address is no longer Optimistic and becomes Preferred or Deprecated.

In the collision case, the address is already in use by another node. The solicitation is sent from the unspecified address with no link-layer address option, so it does not change neighbouring caches. The node can still send a Router Solicitation to ask for more information, but without the option, which forces an all-nodes multicast response and does not disrupt other caches. When a Neighbor Advertisement is received from the node defending the address, the Optimistic Node immediately stops using the address and deconfigures it. The RFC notes that in the meantime the node may have sent packets that identify it as the owner, which may incur broken connections and cause the rightful owner to receive misdirected packets, which is why Optimistic Duplicate Address Detection should be used only where the probability of collision is very low.

Interoperation cases only arise while the address is Optimistic, because afterwards it acts exactly like a normal address. If an Optimistic Node attempts to configure an address currently tentatively assigned to a Standard Node, the Standard Node sees the solicitation and deconfigures the address. If a node attempts to configure an Optimistic Node's address, the Optimistic Node sees the solicitation and deconfigures it.

The pathological cases resemble those of Standard Duplicate Address Detection: duplicates are not guaranteed to be detected if packets are lost. Their probability can be reduced by increasing the RFC 2462 DupAddrDetectTransmits variable to greater than 1. This version of Optimistic Duplicate Address Detection also depends on the details of router behaviour, such as the router including link-layer address options in Router Advertisements and being willing to redirect traffic for the node. Where the router does not behave in this way, the behaviour inherently reverts to that of Standard Duplicate Address Detection.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the check finds nothing and the address simply works. If the address is already taken, the other device says so and the new one drops the address immediately. The check itself can still be defeated by lost packets, exactly as the standard check can.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There are existing security concerns with Neighbor Discovery and Stateless Address Autoconfiguration, and this memo does not purport to fix them. However, it does not significantly increase security concerns either. Secure Neighbor Discovery provides protection against the threats to Neighbor Discovery described in RFC 3756, and Optimistic Duplicate Address Detection introduces no additional threats to Neighbor Discovery if SEND is used.

The memo takes steps to ensure that if another node is already using an address, the proper link-layer address in existing Neighbor Cache entries is not replaced with the link-layer address of the Optimistic Node. There are still scenarios where incorrect entries may be created, if only temporarily. For example, if a router sends out a Neighbor Solicitation for an address while forwarding a packet, the Optimistic Node may respond first, and if the router has no pre-existing link-layer address for that IP address it will accept the response and incorrectly forward any queued packets to the Optimistic Node, which may then respond in an incorrect manner, such as sending a TCP RST in response to an unknown TCP connection. Such transient conditions should be short-lived in most cases.

Likewise, an Optimistic Node can still inject IP packets into the Internet that will in effect be spoofed packets appearing to come from the legitimate node. In some cases those packets may lead to errors or other operational problems, though one would expect upper-layer protocols to treat such packets robustly, in the same way they must treat old and other duplicate packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not make Neighbor Discovery less safe, and it adds no new threats when Secure Neighbor Discovery is used. There can still be a short window where a router sends a packet to the wrong device, but that is transient.

sections.title: Probability of Collision (Appendix A)
sections.content:
Appendix A assesses the usefulness of Duplicate Address Detection by considering the probability of a collision. SLAAC and DHCPv6 both try to guarantee uniqueness, but the uniqueness of SLAAC depends on the reliability of the manufacturing process and on human factors if link-layer addresses can be manually assigned, and the uniqueness of DHCPv6-assigned addresses relies on correct implementation.

Privacy Extensions to SLAAC picks an interface identifier at random from 2^62 possible 64-bit identifiers, allowing for the reserved U and G bits. No attempt is made to guarantee uniqueness, but the probability can be easily estimated. Using the Birthday Paradox formula, an upper bound on the probability that two nodes collide is 5.4e-14 for a network of 500 nodes, 5.4e-12 for 5000, 5.4e-10 for 50000 and 5.4e-08 for 500000.

For an individual node the Birthday Paradox is not needed. When a node moves into a network with K existing nodes, the probability that it will not collide with any of the distinct addresses in use is 1-K/N, so over M moves the probability of causing at least one collision is 1 minus (1-k/n) raised to the power m. Even considering a very large number of moves, 600000, which is slightly more than one move per minute for one year, and rather crowded networks of 50000 nodes per network, the odds of collision for a given node are vanishingly small: 6.66e-10 for 5000-node networks and 6.53e-09 for 50000-node networks. Each collision affects two nodes, so the probability of being affected is twice this. Even if a node moves into networks of 50000 nodes once per minute for 100 years, the probability of causing or suffering a collision at any point is a little over 1 in a million, expressed in the appendix as 1.3e-06.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix shows that collisions are rare. With a randomly chosen address, two nodes on a link of 50000 machines have a chance of collision of at most 5.4e-10. A device that moves every minute for a hundred years still has a chance of causing or suffering a collision of 1.3e-06.
